overview: This period's genuinely new signal is the emergence of autonomous safety planning and visual reasoning work that treats perception, planning, and control as selective, closed-loop processes rather than monolithic end-to-end inference. The fastest acceleration is still in memory-tiered LLM serving: the memory-systems work and the KV-cache adaptation work are converging on bandwidth and capacity walls as the defining constraint for long-context and agentic workloads. LLM evaluation remains active, but the sharper development is not another benchmark; it is explicit auditing of judge dependence, contamination, and selective-label bias. The dense vision and VLM clusters reinforce the same efficiency story from the perception side, while GPU-native reactive robot planning appears to be stalling as a distinct direction. Worth noting: last week's agent attack surfaces in tool runtimes cluster dropped out, suggesting the security conversation has paused while reliability and systems bottlenecks take mindshare.

macro_patterns.name: Memory-tiered inference
macro_patterns.summary: The memory systems for LLM inference cluster and the input-adaptive KV memory management cluster are converging on the same point: long-context and agentic serving are no longer FLOP-bound first, but constrained by KV-cache capacity, off-chip bandwidth, and the latency penalty of moving state across PCIe/CXL/fabric. Recent papers split the problem into explicit memory pipelines, learned eviction/quantization, and disaggregated tiered memory, which is a stronger convergence than last week's isolated optimization work.
macro_patterns.so_what: Serving margin shifts from raw compute throughput to memory-bandwidth allocation and state-placement policy; long-context inference becomes a systems problem before it is a model problem.

macro_patterns.name: Active perception over full-scene reading
macro_patterns.summary: The autonomous planning cluster, the visual reasoning cluster, and the dense vision cluster are all moving away from uniform processing of the full input toward selective, decision-coupled sensing: active frame selection in VLMs, adaptive cropping in dense vision, and fast-slow planning or joint prediction-planning in robotics. The shared constraint is latency under real-time control loops or dense visual inputs, where reading everything at full fidelity is too slow to close the loop.
macro_patterns.so_what: Advantage shifts to systems that decide what not to read; full-resolution, full-context perception becomes an avoidable tax in robotics and multimodal inference.

macro_patterns.name: Evaluation under dependence
macro_patterns.summary: The LLM evaluation cluster and the mechanism-aware forecasting evaluation cluster both reject leaderboard-style scoring in favor of diagnostics that model hidden dependence: entangled judges and contamination in LLM evaluation, intrinsic predictability and mechanism-specific stress regimes in forecasting. The common non-research constraint is procurement risk: buyers need evidence that survives benchmark gaming and correlated failure, not another average score.
macro_patterns.so_what: Benchmark wins lose purchasing power when evaluation itself is treated as a biased instrument; trust shifts to systems that expose where models fail, not just how often.

clusters.label: Disaggregated LLM memory systems
clusters.one_line: This cluster studies hardware-software co-design for long-context and agentic LLM inference where KV state, retrieval memory, and serving stages are spread across heterogeneous memory tiers and devices.
clusters.existing_landscape: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, LMCache, and vendors such as NVIDIA and AMD already cover mainstream LLM serving, KV-cache reuse, and some prefill/decode disaggregation. Cloud providers and inference platforms like Fireworks and Together also optimize long-context serving, but their public stacks still largely assume GPU-attached HBM is the primary high-performance state store and treat external memory as an offload path rather than a first-class scheduling substrate. CXL vendors, DPUs, and storage systems exist, but they are not exposed as integrated inference products with end-to-end state placement semantics.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The research direction has moved beyond simple KV offload: papers like Understand and Accelerate Memory Processing Pipeline for Disaggregated LLM Inference and ITME model inference as a multi-stage memory pipeline with heterogeneous compute, retrieval, and apply phases. None of the named serving stacks expose memory processing as an explicit optimization target spanning GPU HBM, CXL pools, NVMe-oF, and shared context layers; they mostly optimize token scheduling inside a server. That is a mismatch because agentic and long-context workloads are now defined by state movement cost, not just matrix multiply throughput, and existing products still hide memory tiering behind generic cache/offload abstractions.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new and large, and its representative papers are unusually concrete about measured overheads: one reports 22%-97% memory-processing overhead in inference, while ITME and SuperInfer frame TB-scale context state and SLO failures as immediate serving issues rather than future hardware speculation.
clusters.risks: NVIDIA, vLLM, or a cloud inference provider could absorb much of this as a serving-layer feature, especially if CXL and disaggregated memory become standard deployment targets. The gap also depends on long-context and agentic demand persisting at production scale rather than staying concentrated in demos and premium workloads.

clusters.label: Real-time safe adaptive planning
clusters.one_line: This cluster centers on autonomous navigation and vehicle control methods that combine online uncertainty estimation, safety guarantees, and fast hierarchical planning under tight real-time constraints.
clusters.existing_landscape: NVIDIA Isaac, ROS navigation stacks, Autoware, Waymo-style internal autonomy stacks, and industrial MPC vendors already cover planning, control, and simulation-heavy validation. Applied robotics companies and AV programs also use control barrier functions, MPC, and learned prediction modules, while PX4/Crazyflie-style ecosystems support high-rate control for drones. What these systems mostly share is a clean separation between slow offline tuning and fast online control, with conservative safety margins when uncertainty becomes interactive or distribution-shifted.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The recent papers are converging on online-updated safety structure rather than static safety envelopes: learning-based reachable set barriers, adversarially robust conformal prediction under policy-induced distribution shift, and joint prediction-planning diffusion where the robot plan feeds back into predicted multi-agent futures. Shipping stacks rarely expose this kind of adaptive safety contract in real time; they either freeze prediction models and verify against them, or let learned policies act with weak runtime guarantees. That leaves a gap between research showing less conservative, interaction-aware safety updates and industry systems that still pay a heavy efficiency tax to keep safety certifiable.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new and one of the strongest week-over-week risers. The sharpest signal is that multiple papers attack the same failure mode from different angles: policy-induced distribution shift breaks static guarantees, and researchers are now treating that as the core interface problem between planning and safety.
clusters.risks: Waymo, NVIDIA Isaac, or major AV/robotics stacks could incorporate adaptive barrier updates or conformal wrappers as incremental features rather than platform changes. Real-world certification and liability requirements also slow adoption even when the methods work technically.

clusters.label: Auditable LLM evaluation
clusters.one_line: This cluster focuses on evaluating LLMs when judges are correlated, benchmarks are contaminated, and human labels are sparse or selectively applied.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI Evals, Anthropic's internal eval practices, HELM, LM Arena, Scale AI evaluation services, LangSmith, Patronus, Galileo, and Humanloop already cover benchmark runs, human review workflows, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines. These products overlap heavily on prompt-based scoring, red teaming, and leaderboard-style reporting, and most assume that using multiple models or dynamic prompts is enough to stabilize the signal. Even stronger offerings still treat evaluator dependence and selective-label bias as secondary concerns rather than first-order statistical objects.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The research is surfacing a harder problem than benchmark freshness: evaluator agreement is often correlated because models share data, distillation lineage, and alignment style, so 'ensemble' validation can be pseudo-independent. Papers on behavioral entanglement auditing and positive-unlabeled evaluation show capabilities that current tooling generally does not expose: estimating judge dependence, correcting verifier ensemble weights, and auditing evaluation bias when only a small set of positives has human confirmation. That is a meaningful mismatch for enterprise procurement because many commercial eval stacks present confidence without modeling whether their judges fail together.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new, and several papers sharpen the gap beyond generic 'eval is hard' claims. The most important shift is from building more benchmarks to statistically auditing the evaluation process itself, especially in LLMEval-Fair, the behavioral entanglement work, and the PU-learning auditing paper.
clusters.risks: This gap can close quickly because vendors like Scale AI, LangSmith, or Patronus can add dependence diagnostics and bias correction into existing evaluation suites. Some of the newest methods also rely on assumptions that may be hard to validate across proprietary frontier models.

clusters.label: Active visual grounding in VLMs
clusters.one_line: This cluster pushes vision-language models from passive single-pass captioning toward iterative, geometry-aware, and selectively sampled visual reasoning across video and 3D scenes.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and xAI ship multimodal models that answer questions over images and sometimes video, while open models like LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and Video-LLaVA cover the OSS side. Labelbox, Twelve Labs, and standard video analytics vendors support retrieval and tagging, but most shipped systems still rely on uniform frame sampling, static visual tokenization, or external detectors for grounding. Even strong multimodal products generally assume vision is a fixed context presented once to a language model.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The representative papers repeatedly break that assumption: V-Reflection re-queries visual evidence during reasoning, Video Active Perception adaptively selects frames based on information gain, and the 3D grounding work separates semantic reasoning from deterministic geometry instantiation. None of the mainstream APIs expose multimodal inference as an interactive evidence-acquisition loop with explicit geometry or attention-budget control. The gap matters because video and multi-image workloads hit token, latency, and cost ceilings quickly; passive ingestion of all visual context does not scale.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new, and the convergence is tighter than generic multimodal growth: several papers independently argue that static visual encoding is the bottleneck, not just model size. The active frame-selection and reflective grounding papers make the latency-cost constraint explicit.
clusters.risks: Frontier model providers can productize active visual querying as an inference strategy without changing the model API much, which would narrow the gap fast. Some gains may also be benchmark-specific if interactive perception overhead outweighs savings on short inputs.

clusters.label: Adaptive KV state compression
clusters.one_line: This cluster develops learned eviction, quantization, and hybrid-attention methods to reduce KV-cache growth and continual adaptation interference in long-context LLMs.
clusters.existing_landscape: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, Hugging Face TGI, MLC, and vendor kernels already support paging, prefix caching, quantization, and some attention optimizations for long-context inference. Compression startups and OSS projects increasingly expose fixed-policy cache quantization or heuristic eviction, and model providers train longer-context variants directly. The common assumption across shipped systems is that cache management is mostly heuristic, model-agnostic, and subordinate to the serving engine rather than learned from the workload.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Recent papers such as IndexMem and adaptive KV-cache quantization argue that token importance is input-dependent enough to justify learned retention and precision allocation, while LightTransfer suggests converting pretrained transformers into hybrid architectures instead of merely serving them more cleverly. Current inference stacks largely expose static knobs, not per-request learned memory policies tied to model internals or downstream task structure. As context lengths rise, that assumption clashes with evidence that memory mistakes are no longer random degradation but a controllable quality-cost tradeoff.
clusters.why_now: The cluster is stable rather than newly accelerating, but it remains strategically important because it now complements the newer disaggregated memory-systems work. The combination makes the bottleneck clearer: one line optimizes where state lives, the other what state deserves to exist at all.
clusters.risks: This is the kind of systems feature vLLM, NVIDIA, or model vendors can absorb directly, which limits standalone novelty. Some learned policies may also prove too model-specific or operationally brittle for broad deployment.

dropped_clusters.label: Agent attack surfaces in tool runtimes
dropped_clusters.one_line: This cluster studies how prompt injection, poisoned tool metadata, jailbreak automation, and guardrail denial-of-service emerge specifically in deployed agent systems rather than base models alone.
